title: Kangaroo Mother Care
subject: Paediatrics
summary: Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC) is skin‑to‑skin contact, exclusive breastfeeding and follow‑up for preterm or low‑birth‑weight infants. It improves thermoregulation, stabilises physiology and reduces mortality, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Skin‑to‑skin contact ≥18 h/day
Exclusive breastfeeding or expressed breast‑milk
Daily weight monitoring and parental education

sections.p: KMC is not staged like a disease, but infants are categorised by stability to decide when to start:
b: Stable: warm, breathing spontaneously, no apnea, no infection – start KMC immediately
Unstable: respiratory distress, hypoglycaemia, sepsis – stabilise in NICU before KMC

sections.p: The need for KMC arises from prematurity and low birth weight, which are common in East Africa due to maternal malnutrition, infections and limited antenatal care.
b: Maternal malaria or HIV infection → preterm birth
Maternal undernutrition or anemia → intra‑uterine growth restriction
Multiple pregnancy, obstetric complications

sections.p: A newborn eligible for KMC will be small for gestational age, with thin, translucent skin, minimal subcutaneous fat and a high surface‑area‑to‑mass ratio. Clinically they may have cool extremities and risk of hypoglycaemia.
b: Temperature <36.5 °C if not in skin‑to‑skin contact
Feeding difficulty due to immature suck

sections.p: Investigations focus on confirming stability and ruling out infection; many may be unavailable in low‑resource settings.

t.b: Is the infant hypoglycaemic? <2.5 mmol/L indicates need for glucose supplementation before KMC.
Is the infant normothermic? <36.5 °C requires warming before prolonged skin‑to‑skin.
Is there leukocytosis or neutropenia suggesting infection? Treat sepsis before KMC.
Is SpO₂ ≥90 % on room air? Low saturation signals respiratory compromise; stabilize first.

sections.p: Although KMC is safe, certain signs demand urgent medical review.
b: Persistent temperature <35 °C despite skin‑to‑skin
Apnoea or bradycardia episodes
Severe jaundice (bilirubin >250 µmol/L) or rapid rise
Signs of infection: lethargy, poor feeding, fever >38 °C

sections.p: Start KMC once the infant is stable; combine with supportive measures and parental education.
b: Skin‑to‑skin: mother (or father) holds infant upright on chest, covered with a blanket; aim ≥18 h/day
Breast‑milk feeding: encourage on‑demand, monitor weight daily; if insufficient, express milk and supplement with donor milk if available
Thermal monitoring: check temperature every 2 h for first 24 h
Infection control: hand‑washing before handling, clean cord care with sterile technique

sections.p: Regular community or clinic visits ensure growth and early detection of problems.
b: Weekly weight checks for the first month, then fortnightly until 6 weeks
Counselling on exclusive breastfeeding, danger signs and immunisations
Referral for persistent growth failure or recurrent illness

sections.p: KMC may be mistaken for simple “incubator care” or “warm chain” alone.
b: Incubator: provides external heat but no skin‑to‑skin contact or breastfeeding support
Warm chain: includes drying, wrapping and room temperature control but not prolonged contact

sections.p: In low‑resource settings some measurements may appear normal despite risk.
b: Normal axillary temperature can mask peripheral cooling if the infant is covered inadequately
Weight gain of 10 g/day may seem adequate but could hide dehydration if fluid balance is not assessed

whenToSeekHelp: Severe jaundice or rapid bilirubin rise
Signs of sepsis (fever, lethargy, poor feeding)

faq.a: It provides warmth, stabilises heart rate and breathing, promotes breastfeeding and improves neurodevelopment.
Yes, any caregiver can hold the baby skin‑to‑skin; this increases bonding and allows mothers to rest.

faq.q: What if the mother cannot breast‑feed?
faq.a: Expressed breast‑milk or donor milk should be used; formula is a last resort in low‑resource settings.

exam: What physiological changes occur in a preterm infant during skin‑to‑skin contact — stabilisation of temperature, heart rate, respiratory pattern and glucose levels.
Explain why exclusive breastfeeding is a core component of KMC — it supplies optimal nutrition, immunoglobulins and promotes gut maturation, reducing infection risk.

You have no pulse oximeter. How would you assess respiratory stability before starting KMC — observe work of breathing, chest rise, colour, and count respiratory rate; if >60/min with grunting, delay KMC.
List three danger signs that require urgent referral of a baby on KMC — persistent hypothermia, apnoea/bradycardia, severe jaundice.
How would you counsel a mother who fears that KMC will expose her baby to infection — explain that skin‑to‑skin improves immune function, and hand‑washing prevents transmission.

Differentiate KMC from incubator care in terms of long‑term neurodevelopmental outcomes — KMC shows better bonding, reduced stress hormones and improved cognitive scores, while incubators lack these benefits.
A mother with HIV wants to practice KMC. What advice do you give regarding transmission — KMC is safe; continue antiretroviral therapy and exclusive breastfeeding as per WHO guidelines.
